procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Criminal Appeal filed by the Appellants challenging the conviction under Section 302/201 IPC was considered. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no infirmity in the findings of the Trial Court and High Court.

directions: The appellants, if enlarged on bail, shall surrender before the concerned Jail Superintendent within two weeks from the date of this judgment for serving their sentence.
Registry to communicate the order forthwith.
Interim application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Whether the findings of the High Court, upholding the conviction under Section 302/201 IPC, are based on a correct appreciation of the evidence and are sustainable in law.

facts: The appellants were convicted by the Trial Court for offences under Sections 302 (murder) and 201 (causing disappearance of evidence) of the Indian Penal Code, based on circumstantial evidence.
The High Court dismissed their appeal, upholding the Trial Court's conviction and finding that the evidence had been correctly analyzed.
The appellants then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the lower courts had failed to properly appreciate the evidence and circumstances of the case.
law: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances proved must unequivocally point to the guilt of the accused and be incompatible with any theory of their innocence.
Evidence must be examined as a whole and not in isolated parts. In circumstantial cases, the court must analyze the proved circumstances collectively to draw an irresistible inference.

Minor variations or contradictions in witness testimonies are not fatal to the prosecution's case, as natural testimony is bound to have variations. The court must consider the social position of the witness and not subject their testimony to mathematical precision.
The Supreme Court will not disturb the consistent findings of two lower courts (Trial Court and High Court) unless there is a finding of illegality, perversity, or impossibility in their conclusions.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the evidence and found that both the Trial Court and the High Court had correctly appreciated it.
It found no material contradictions in the witness testimonies, noting that the witnesses were villagers and their statements should not be scrutinized with mathematical precision.

The Court determined that when the evidence was examined collectively and comprehensively, the circumstantial evidence was consistent and overwhelmingly pointed towards the guilt of the appellants, leaving no room for an alternate possibility of their innocence.
The Court concluded that there was no illegality, perversity, or infirmity in the concurrent findings of the lower courts that would warrant interference.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appeal, holding that the High Court's findings were based on a correct appreciation of the evidence and were sustainable in law. Since the consistent views of the two lower courts were not found to be illegal or perverse, the Supreme Court upheld the conviction and dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the findings of the High Court, upholding the conviction under Section 302/201 IPC, are based on a correct appreciation of the evidence and are sustainable in law.
appellant_arguments: The trial court and the High Court failed to properly analyze the circumstances of the case, which was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
respondent_arguments: The trial court and the High Court correctly analyzed the evidence on record, and the findings establishing a consistent chain of evidence pointing to the appellants' guilt were sound and free from infirmity.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the proven circumstances must be of a conclusive nature, pointing unequivocally to the guilt of the accused and being incompatible with any theory of innocence. The established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt and not explainable by any other. The evidence must be examined as a whole, not in isolation, to analyze the proven circumstances collectively and draw an irresistible inference. The mere presence of minor variations in testimony is not fatal to the prosecution's case, as natural testimony is bound to have variations.
obiter: The evidence of every witness cannot be subject to the same level of scrutiny, and the Court must be alive to the social position of the witness.
In the absence of a finding of illegality, perversity, or impossibility, consistent views taken by two lower courts cannot be disturbed on mere conjectures or surmises.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court held that the Trial Court and High Court had correctly appreciated the evidence on record, and in the absence of any finding of illegality, perversity, or impossibility in their consistent findings, those views cannot be disturbed. When the entire evidence is examined collectively and comprehensively, the only possibility that emerges is the guilt of the appellants, which is an irresistible inference drawn from the proved material on record.
legal_tests_applied: When a case is based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established; (2) the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused; (3) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency; (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
The circumstances concerned “must or should” and not “may be” established.

The evidence adduced before the Court is to be examined as a whole and not in isolation. This principle assumes greater importance in cases which are based on circumstantial evidence as in the absence of direct evidence of the offence, the Court is required to analyze the proved circumstances in a collective sense so as to arrive at a reasonable finding.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants' attempt to raise questions regarding the evidence of individual witnesses for isolated reasons was rejected, as the court held that evidence must be examined as a whole and not in isolation, especially in a circumstantial evidence case.
The Court found no illegality, perversity, or impossibility in the impugned findings of the lower courts.
The Court refused to disturb the consistent views taken by two lower courts on the basis of mere conjectures or surmises.
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court affirmed the lower courts' findings, stating that they had correctly appreciated the evidence on record and that their findings were sustainable in the eyes of law.
The Court found that when the entire evidence led by the prosecution is examined collectively and comprehensively, the only possibility that emerges is of the guilt of the appellants.

The Court concluded that the finding of guilt was an irresistible inference drawn from the proved material on record, which formed a complete chain of evidence consistent only with the hypothesis of guilt.
policy_considerations: In cases based on circumstantial evidence, it is crucial to analyze the proved circumstances in a collective sense to arrive at a reasonable finding, rather than examining evidence in isolation.
Consistent factual findings by two lower courts should not be disturbed by a higher court unless there is a clear finding of illegality, perversity, or impossibility.

Natural testimony is bound to have minor variations, and their mere presence is not fatal to the prosecution's case; the evidence of every witness cannot be subject to the same level of scrutiny, and the court must be alive to the social position of the witness.
